arXiv:2407.10218v1 [math.AP] 14 Jul 2024

Wavefronts for a degenerate reaction-diffusion system with application to bacterial growth models

Luisa Malaguti    Elisa Sovrano ††thanks: The authors are members of the Gruppo Nazionale per l’Analisi Matematica, la Probabilità e le loro Applicazioni (GNAMPA) of the Istituto Nazionale di Alta Matematica (INdAM) and acknowledge financial support from this institution and the PRIN 2022 project Modeling, Control and Games through Partial Differential Equations (D53D23005620006), funded by the European Union - Next Generation EU.
Abstract

We investigate wavefront solutions in a nonlinear system of two coupled reaction-diffusion equations with degenerate diffusivity:

nt=nx​x−n​b,bt=[D​n​b​bx]x+n​b,n_{t}=n_{xx}-nb,\hskip 9.24994ptb_{t}=[Dnbb_{x}]_{x}+nb,

where t≥0,t\geq 0, x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, and DD is a positive diffusion coefficient. This model, introduced by Kawasaki et al. (J. Theor. Biol. 188, 1997), describes the spatial-temporal dynamics of bacterial colonies b=b⁡(x,t)b=b(x,t) and nutrients n=n⁡(x,t)n=n(x,t) on agar plates. Kawasaki et al. provided numerical evidence for wavefronts, leaving the analytical confirmation of these solutions an open problem. We prove the existence of an infinite family of wavefronts parameterized by their wave speed, which varies on a closed positive half-line. We provide an upper bound for the threshold speed and a lower bound for it when DD is sufficiently large. The proofs are based on several analytical tools, including the shooting method and the fixed-point theory in Fréchet spaces, to establish existence, and the central manifold theorem to ascertain uniqueness.

Mathematics Subject Classifications: 35C07, 35K55, 35K57.

Keywords: degenerate diffusion, reaction-diffusion equations, wavefront, wave speed.

1 Introduction and main results

In this article, we are exploring a nonlinear system of two coupled reaction-diffusion equations that models the growth of bacteria on agar plates with nutrients. Based on laboratory experiments and numerical analyses, it has been observed that bacterial evolution can produce various spatiotemporal patterns during bacterial growth, including rings, disks, and dense branching morphologies, which depend on the bacterial species and nutrient conditions (see [9, 12, 13, 18]). To study the evolution of bacteria and nutrients, we consider the reaction-diffusion model as described in [13]:

nt=Dn​nx​x−n​b,\displaystyle n_{t}=D_{n}n_{xx}-nb, (1.1a)
bt=[Db​n​b​bx]x+n​b,\displaystyle b_{t}=[D_{b}nbb_{x}]_{x}+nb, (1.1b)

where n=n⁡(x,t)n=n(x,t) and b=b⁡(x,t)b=b(x,t) are the concentration of the nutrient and the population density of bacteria, respectively, at time t≥0t\geq 0 and space x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. The parameters DnD_{n} and DbD_{b} are the nutrient and bacteria diffusion coefficients, respectively. The diffusivity of bacteria is nonlinear and degenerates to model its trend toward reduced mobility when the nutrient or the bacteria concentration level is low (i.e., if either nn or bb tends to zero).

Experimental observations reported in [13] have shown that system (1.1b) can generate spatiotemporal patterns supported by traveling wave solutions. These solutions are characterized by profiles that propagate at a constant speed, specifically represented by:

n⁡(x,t)=η⁡(x−c​t),b⁡(x,t)=β⁡(x−c​t),n(x,t)=\eta(x-ct),\quad b(x,t)=\beta(x-ct), (1.2)

where (η,β)(\eta,\beta) represents the profile and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} denotes the wave speed, which is an unknown of the problem. Despite these experimental observations, there is a lack of theoretical proof for the existence of traveling wave solutions for system (1.1b), nor has there been an analytical study of the admissible wave speeds. This work aims to address these theoretical and analytical gaps.

In [20], researchers analyzed the case Dn=0D_{n}=0 and, through both numerical and analytical approaches, indicated that wavefronts display “sharp” behavior in the bacteria profile at a critical speed (see Definition 1.2). In [19], the studied system is

{nt=−f⁡(n,b),bt=[g⁡(n)​h​(b)​bx]x+f⁡(n,b),\begin{cases}n_{t}=-f(n,b),\\ b_{t}=[g(n)h(b)b_{x}]_{x}+f(n,b),\end{cases}

where the diffusion term g⁡(n)​h​(b)g(n)h(b) degenerates at both n=0n=0 and b=0b=0, and the reaction term f⁡(n,b)f(n,b) is positive except when n=0n=0 or b=0b=0. They established the existence of wavefronts for all wave speeds within a closed half-line and, similar to the model in [20], showed that the profile exhibits “sharp” behavior at the threshold speed. It has been also demonstrated in [19] that the profiles for all other speeds are smooth. For the classical non-degenerate case, the analogous system studied in literature is:

{nt=λ​nx​x−f⁡(n,b),bt=bx​x+f⁡(n,b),\begin{cases}n_{t}=\lambda n_{xx}-f(n,b),\\ b_{t}=b_{xx}+f(n,b),\end{cases}

where λ≥0\lambda\geq 0. Results depend on different properties of the function ff, which is consistently assumed to be as before (see, e.g., [1, 2, 4, 5, 15, 17]). This model applies to contexts such as modeling an isothermal autocatalytic chemical reaction (where nn and bb represent the concentrations of the autocatalysts) or modeling thermal diffusive combustion (where nn is the concentration of the reactant and bb is the temperature of the mixture). Various results regarding wavefronts have been obtained depending on the value of λ\lambda and the properties of ff. If λ=0\lambda=0 or λ>0\lambda>0 and f⁡(n,b)=n​bf(n,b)=nb, an admissible closed half-line of wave speeds has been demonstrated (see [4, 15]). Conversely, if λ>0\lambda>0 and f​(n,b)=g~​(n)​bf(n,b)=\tilde{g}(n)b with g~​(0)=0\tilde{g}(0)=0 and g~​(s)>0\tilde{g}(s)>0 for all s∈(0,1]s\in(0,1], then an admissible closed half-line of wave speeds is guaranteed for 0<λ<10<\lambda<1 (see [17]). For λ>1\lambda>1, however, the set of admissible speeds may be disconnected (see [5]). These results have been further improved in [1] to include more general reaction terms f⁡(n,b)f(n,b).

Without loss of generality, in the following, we assume in (1.1b) that

Dn=1andDb=D>0.D_{n}=1\quad\text{and}\quad D_{b}=D>0.

When introducing the wave coordinate ξ:=x−c​t\xi:=x-ct, the functions η\eta and β\beta in (1.2) satisfy the system

η′′+c​η′−η​β=0,\displaystyle\eta^{\prime\prime}+c\eta^{\prime}-\eta\beta=0, (1.3a)
(D​η​β​β′)′+c​β′+η​β=0,\displaystyle\left(D\eta\beta\beta^{\prime}\right)^{\prime}+c\beta^{\prime}+\eta\beta=0, (1.3b)

where ′=dd​ξ{}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\xi}. The nontrivial stationary solutions associated with (1.3b) belong to one of the following sets:

{(η,β):η≡Kη,β≡0, with Kη∈(0,+∞)},{(η,β):η≡0,β≡Kβ, with Kβ∈(0,+∞)}.\{(\eta,\beta)\colon\eta\equiv K_{\eta},\,\beta\equiv 0,\text{ with }K_{\eta}\in(0,+\infty)\},\quad\{(\eta,\beta)\colon\eta\equiv 0,\,\beta\equiv K_{\beta},\text{ with }K_{\beta}\in(0,+\infty)\}.

Here, we look for traveling waves of (1.1b) that connect nontrivial stationary solutions characterized by profiles (η,β)(\eta,\beta) consisting of a pair of strictly monotone functions (i.e., wavefronts). In the following, we will consider Kη=1=KβK_{\eta}=1=K_{\beta} and look for wavefronts that connect the two stationary solutions (0,1)(0,1) and (1,0)(1,0). This leads to the boundary conditions:

(η⁡(−∞),β⁡(−∞))=(0,1),\displaystyle\left(\eta(-\infty),\beta(-\infty)\right)=(0,1), (1.4a)
(η⁡(+∞),β⁡(+∞))=(1,0),\displaystyle\left(\eta(+\infty),\beta(+\infty)\right)=(1,0), (1.4b)

where for any function m⁡(ξ)m(\xi) with a limit at ±∞\pm\infty, we abbreviate limξ→±∞m⁡(ξ)=m⁡(±∞)\lim_{\xi\to\pm\infty}m(\xi)=m(\pm\infty).

Given the presence of a degenerate diffusion term in system (1.1b), before stating our results, let us point out the solution notion we are seeking (see [8]).

Definition 1.1 (Wavefront and semi-wavefront).

Let J⊆ℝJ\subseteq\mathbb{R} be an open interval and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}. Consider two non-constant monotone functions η,β:J→ℝ\eta,\beta\colon J\to\mathbb{R} such that

  1. (i)(i)

    η\eta is of class C2C^{2} and solves (1.3a);

  2. (i​i)(ii)

    β\beta is continuous and differentiable a.e. with β​β′∈Ll​o​c1​(J)\beta\beta^{\prime}\in L^{1}_{loc}(J) and solves weakly (1.3b), namely, for every ψ∈C0∞​(J)\psi\in C^{\infty}_{0}(J), it satisfies

    ∫J[(D​η​(ξ)​β​(ξ)​β′​(ξ)+c​β​(ξ))​ψ′​(ξ)−η⁡(ξ)​β​(ξ)​ψ​(ξ)]​𝑑ξ=0.\int_{J}\left[\left(D\eta(\xi)\beta(\xi)\beta^{\prime}(\xi)+c\beta(\xi)\right)\psi^{\prime}(\xi)-\eta(\xi)\beta(\xi)\psi(\xi)\right]\,\mathrm{d}\xi=0. (1.5)
  • •

    When J=ℝJ=\mathbb{R} and (η,β)(\eta,\beta) satisfies (1.4b), (n,b)(n,b) with n⁡(x,t)=η⁡(x−c​t)=η⁡(ξ)n(x,t)=\eta(x-ct)=\eta(\xi) and b⁡(x,t)=β⁡(x−c​t)=β⁡(ξ)b(x,t)=\beta(x-ct)=\beta(\xi) is called (global) wavefront of (1.1b).

  • •

    When J=(−∞,a)J=(-\infty,a) (or J=(a,+∞)J=(a,+\infty)) with a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R} and (η,β)(\eta,\beta) satisfies (1.4a) (or (1.4b)), (n,b)(n,b) with n⁡(x,t)=η⁡(x−c​t)=η⁡(ξ)n(x,t)=\eta(x-ct)=\eta(\xi) and b⁡(x,t)=β⁡(x−c​t)=β⁡(ξ)b(x,t)=\beta(x-ct)=\beta(\xi) is called semi-wavefront in JJ of (1.1b).

In both cases, the pair (η,β)(\eta,\beta) denotes the wave profile of (n,b)(n,b), whereas cc stands for the wave speed.

Warning. For conciseness, we will refer also to the profile (η,β)(\eta,\beta) as “wavefront” of (1.1b) or “semi-wavefront” of (1.1b) (satisfying either (1.4a) or (1.4b)).

Definition 1.2 (Classical and sharp wavefront).

A wavefront (η,β)(\eta,\beta) is said to be classical if the function β\beta is differentiable, β​β′\beta\beta^{\prime} is absolutely continuous, and the equation (1.3b) holds a.e. On the other hand, a wavefront (η,β)(\eta,\beta) is said to be sharp at the point ℓ∈{0,1}\ell\in\{0,1\} if there exists a real number ξℓ\xi_{\ell} such that β⁡(ξℓ)=ℓ\beta(\xi_{\ell})=\ell, and the function β\beta is classical on the set ℝ∖{ξℓ}\mathbb{R}\setminus\{\xi_{\ell}\}, but not differentiable at the point ξℓ\xi_{\ell}.

This work investigates conditions under which wavefronts exist and examines their regularity properties. Specifically, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of a semi-wavefront for each positive wave speed in the negative half-line (−∞,0](-\infty,0]. Our approach utilizes shooting method and fixed-point theory in Fréchet spaces to establish existence and the central manifold theorem to ascertain uniqueness.

Theorem 1.1.

Let Dn=1D_{n}=1 and Db=D>0D_{b}=D>0. For each c>0c>0, system (1.1b) has a unique semi-wavefront in (−∞,0](-\infty,0] with wave speed cc whose profile (η,β)(\eta,\beta) satisfies (1.4a). Moreover, η′>0\eta^{\prime}>0 and β′<0\beta^{\prime}<0.

Further, we extend the solution to the positive half-line [0,+∞)[0,+\infty) and show that sufficiently large wave speeds yield a classical global wavefront.

Theorem 1.2.

Let Dn=1D_{n}=1 and Db=D>0D_{b}=D>0. There exists c0>0c_{0}>0 such that, for every c≥c0c\geq c_{0}, system (1.1b) has a unique wavefront with wave speed cc whose profile (η,β)(\eta,\beta) satisfies (1.4b). If c>c0c>c_{0}, the wavefront is classical. Moreover, the following estimates on c0c_{0} hold:

max⁡{0,D/15−1}<c0≤2​D​eD.\max\left\{0,\sqrt{{D}/{15}}-1\right\}<c_{0}\leq 2\sqrt{De^{D}}.

Drawing parallels with the scenario when D=0D=0, we conjecture the existence of a threshold wave speed for which a sharp wavefront for system (1.1b) can be observed (see [19, 20]).

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents preliminary properties of systems (1.3b)–(1.4b) that are essential for further analysis. This section also discusses further formulation of the system provided by equation (2.7), which is ensured by the boundary conditions and the coupling of the reaction term. The proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 are detailed in Sections 3 and 4, respectively.

η0:=η⁡(0),η0′:=η′​(0),β0:=β⁡(0),β0′:=β′​(0).\eta_{0}:=\eta(0),\quad\eta^{\prime}_{0}:=\eta^{\prime}(0),\qquad\beta_{0}:=\beta(0),\quad\beta^{\prime}_{0}:=\beta^{\prime}(0). (2.1)

It is straightforward to demonstrate that, for every ξ0∈ℝ\xi_{0}\in\mathbb{R}, the shifted pair (η(⋅+ξ0),β(⋅+ξ0))\left(\eta(\cdot+\xi_{0}),\beta(\cdot+\xi_{0})\right) remains a solution of (1.3b). β0>0.\beta_{0}>0.

Remark 2.10.

According to Lemma 2.1 (v)(v), the wavefronts (η,β)(\eta,\beta) of (1.1b) satisfy β⁡(ξ)<1\beta(\xi)<1 for every ξ∈ℝ\xi\in\mathbb{R}, which implies that wavefronts can only be sharp at ℓ=0\ell=0 (cf., Definition 1.2). In Proposition 2.12, we will show that the case τ<+∞\tau<+\infty and β′​(τ−)=0\beta^{\prime}(\tau^{-})=0 can not occur. Figure 1 illustrates the two types of admissible wavefronts of (1.1b).

3 Semi-wavefront on the negative half-line

In this section, we demonstrate Theorem 1.1 by proving the existence of a semi-wavefront of (1.1b) with positive speed cc in the half-line (−∞,0](-\infty,0] (as will be shown in Proposition 3.1) and its uniqueness (as will be shown in Proposition 3.10).

Proposition 3.1.

For every c>0c>0, there exists a semi-wavefront (η,β)(\eta,\beta) of (1.1b) in (−∞,0](-\infty,0] with wave speed cc. Moreover, η′​(ξ)>0\eta^{\prime}(\xi)>0 and β′​(ξ)<0\beta^{\prime}(\xi)<0 for all ξ∈(−∞,0]\xi\in(-\infty,0].

The proof is based on comparison results, i.e., we use upper and lower functions (cf., [14]). Let −∞≤a−<a+≤+∞-\infty\leq a_{-}<a_{+}\leq+\infty and let f:(a−,a+)×ℝ×ℝ→ℝf\colon(a_{-},a_{+})\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be a continuous function. We say that yy is a lower function of u′′=f⁡(ξ,u,u′)u^{\prime\prime}=f(\xi,u,u^{\prime}) if y∈C2​(a−,a+)y\in C^{2}(a_{-},a_{+}) and y′′​(ξ)≥f⁡(ξ,y⁡(ξ),y′​(ξ))y^{\prime\prime}(\xi)\geq f\left(\xi,y(\xi),y^{\prime}(\xi)\right) for every ξ∈(a−,a+)\xi\in(a_{-},a_{+}). If the ≥\geq sign is replaced by ≤\leq, we say that yy is an upper function.

We first investigate the solvability of (1.3a) in (−∞,0](-\infty,0] with positive cc and sufficiently regular β\beta and establish some necessary conditions for the existence of semi-wavefronts of (1.1b) on the half-line (−∞,0](-\infty,0].

and also an upper function of (1.3a). We will now prove Proposition 3.1 and establish the existence of a semi-wavefront of (1.1b) in the half-line (−∞,0](-\infty,0] using a fixed-point argument. Proof of Theorem 1.1.

The thesis follows by Propositions 3.1 and 3.10. ∎

In this section, we aim to demonstrate Theorem 1.2. To proceed with the proof of the theorem, we first consider the semi-wavefront (η,β)(\eta,\beta) of (1.1b) in (−∞,0](-\infty,0] with wave speed c>0c>0, whose unique existence is established by Theorem 1.1. Next, we extend this semi-wavefront to the interval [0,τ)[0,\tau), where τ\tau is defined as in (2.2). Notably, η′>0\eta^{\prime}>0 and β′<0\beta^{\prime}<0 hold on (−∞,τ)(-\infty,\tau) (see Lemma 2.1 and Remark 2.2), allowing us to define zc​(β)z_{c}(\beta) for 0<β<10<\beta<1, as described in (2.23), and consider problem (2.24c).

Secondly, we introduce the following auxiliary first-order boundary value problem:

(see [6, Theorem 2.6] and [16, Lemma 2.1]) There exists a positive constant σ∗\sigma^{*} satisfying 0<σ∗≤2​D​eD0<\sigma^{*}\leq 2\sqrt{De^{D}} such that problem (4.1c) has a unique solution if and only if σ≥σ∗\sigma\geq\sigma^{*}. Proposition 4.2.

Let wσ∗w_{\sigma^{*}} be the solution of problem (4.1c) associated with the parameter σ∗\sigma^{*}. Then, for every c≥σ∗c\geq\sigma^{*} the solution zcz_{c} of (2.24c) satisfies

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Let us define c0:=σ∗,c_{0}:=\sigma^{*}, where σ∗\sigma^{*} is the threshold speed associated to (4.1c) (see Proposition 4.1). Consider the semi-wavefront (η,β)(\eta,\beta) of (1.1b) in (−∞,0](-\infty,0] with wave speed c≥c0c\geq c_{0} (see Theorem 1.1) and extend it to [0,τ)[0,\tau).

We consider two cases for τ\tau. If τ=+∞\tau=+\infty, then (η,β)(\eta,\beta) is a classical wavefront of (1.1b) with wave speed cc by Proposition (2.12) (i)(i). On the contrary, if τ<+∞\tau<+\infty, we consider the function zcz_{c} defined in (2.23) which satisfies problem (2.24c). By Proposition (4.2) and Lemma 2.1, we have that

0≥limξ→τ−D​η​(ξ)​β​(ξ)​β′​(ξ)=limβ→0+zc​(β)≥limβ→0+wσ∗​(β)=0;0\geq\lim_{\xi\to\tau^{-}}D\eta(\xi)\beta(\xi)\beta^{\prime}(\xi)=\lim_{\beta\to 0^{+}}z_{c}(\beta)\geq\lim_{\beta\to 0^{+}}w_{\sigma^{*}}(\beta)=0;

hence, (η,β)(\eta,\beta) is a wavefront of (1.1b) with wave speed cc by Proposition 2.12 (i​i)(ii).

We now show that τ<+∞\tau<+\infty is impossible when c>c0c>c_{0}. Indeed, let c>c0c>c_{0}. Notice that z˙c​(0)\dot{z}_{c}(0) exists (see [16, Lemma 2.1]) and it is z˙c​(0)=0\dot{z}_{c}(0)=0 or z˙c​(0)=−c\dot{z}_{c}(0)=-c. Since w˙σ∗=−σ∗\dot{w}_{\sigma^{*}}=-\sigma^{*} (see Proposition 4.1) the latter case is in contradiction with inequality (4.2). Hence z˙c​(0)=0\dot{z}_{c}(0)=0 and then, by (2.23), we obtain

limξ→τ−β′​(ξ)=limβ→0+zc​(β)D​β​η​(ξ⁡(β))=0,\lim_{\xi\to\tau^{-}}\beta^{\prime}(\xi)=\lim_{\beta\to 0^{+}}\frac{z_{c}(\beta)}{D\beta\eta(\xi(\beta))}=0,

which is not compatible with τ<+∞\tau<+\infty (as showed in the proof of Proposition 2.12 (i​i)(ii)).

Finally, we will refer to Propositions 2.7 and 4.1 for comparison estimates of c0c_{0}. This completes the proof. ∎
